_comment: Claude Code project permissions for ai-project-tracker (Cloudflare Wrangler + D1).
This is strict JSON (no // comments allowed), hence this field instead of a header comment.
allow: safe, read-only, or local-only actions. No prompt.
- Read/Grep/Glob/Edit/Write: normal code editing tools.
- git status/diff/log: inspection only, no state change.
- ls/cat/pwd: basic shell inspection.
- wrangler dev: runs the local dev server, no deploy.
- wrangler d1 execute --local: only touches the local SQLite copy of D1
(.wrangler/state), never the remote database. The allow rule is pinned
to the 'tracker' database name (see wrangler.jsonc) with --local right
after it, matching the canonical
`npx wrangler d1 execute tracker --local ...` form.
ask: reversible-but-consequential actions. Always confirm.
- wrangler deploy: this project ships via `git push` (CI/CD), so a manual
deploy from this machine is almost never intended.
- wrangler d1 execute --remote: mutates the production database directly,
bypassing schema review. This rule is pinned to `--remote` (not a bare
'd1 execute:*' catch-all) on purpose: Claude Code's precedence is
deny > ask > allow with NO specificity override, so a broad ask rule
here would shadow the --local allow rule above and force a prompt on
every local D1 command too. Any d1 execute invocation that matches
neither this nor the --local allow rule (wrong db name, unusual flag
order, no flag at all) falls through to the default prompt instead --
covered in normal permission mode, but NOT guaranteed if you ever
switch into acceptEdits/bypassPermissions/auto mode. Type the command
in the canonical form above to stay covered.
- git commit/push: done manually via GitHub Desktop, so Claude should
never commit or push on its own.
curl/wget are deliberately absent from allow, ask, and deny. Claude Code
evaluates permissions as deny > ask > allow, and deny always wins even
against a more specific allow rule -- so a blanket 'deny curl to anything
but localhost' rule isn't expressible (it would block localhost too).
Leaving them unlisted means every curl/wget call, localhost or not, falls
to the default prompt: nothing runs silently, nothing is blocked outright.
deny: never run, no override.
- rm -rf: too easy to catastrophically delete the wrong path.
